utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. I see that Mr. Harmon and Mr. Tieger are representing the Prosecution this morning, and Mr. Josse, you are here to represent Mr. Krajisnik. I've got two technical matters. The first is: Would it be possible for the Prosecution to respond to the motions as we discussed yesterday at the very end of the first session? And how much time would it take?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is possible. Mr. Gaynor will be making the submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then invite him to -- I take it that it would not take more than five, maximum ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take time for that. I have another practical matter and I'm now looking at you, Mr. Josse. There was a specific request from the Defence to alternate morning and afternoon sessions. This always is a bit of a battle. But there is even a chance that we could get even a bit more afternoon sessions, although I know that it's -- for none of us it's our personal preference, but would the Defence, if it would be more than half, would that assist you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I discussed the matter with Mr. Stewart last week after I received a helpful call from one of Your Honour's legal officers, and our conclusion was a half is exactly what we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't want more?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. We don't want more. Could I just say this: That it may be that Mr. Stewart will be here later on to address the Chamber about scheduling matters in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then I have to go back to the -- because I had the impression that sitting in the afternoon would give you more time to prepare also in the Detention Unit and that for that reason it might even be one of your wishes to even have more than half. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I leave the matter open until the end of today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I suspect Mr. Stewart will be listening to this, and if anything, it will make him more, rather than less likely, to come here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from that, whether we can follow your wishes, we have in the month of November, we have a specific problem that only two courtrooms are available for trials ongoing. One of the trials usually scheduled for the morning, for reasons still not fully explained to everyone in this house, so therefore it might be that not in every respect your wish could be followed. There's another matter that it might be alternating not week by week, but half week by half week. That's one of the problems, to do it on a weekly basis or on a two or three days basis. I'll further discuss the matter with the court management. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. After I made that commitment that we could make the submissions at the end of this hour, I realised Mr. Gaynor told me yesterday evening that he will be in a doctor's appointment this morning. So if I could check during the first break, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. We would not call him back -- going to a doctor in the Netherlands usually means that you are spending a lot of time in the waiting-room. We will not call him back neither from the waiting-room or -- but if he would be there, we'd prefer, so if you would check at the end of the first session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd be glad to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, are you ready to continue the examination in chief of the witness Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst we're waiting, could I say copies are being made for the interpreters of these documents at this very moment and I hope they will be supplied within the next 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's good to hear. At the same time, I draw your attention to the fact that with documents, sometimes using the ELMO can help us out. That certainly is not the case for videos, because there we really need a transcript. And I don't think there will be any other video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are no other videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but for the future, I just draw your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasic. Please be seated. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday. May I take it that you not only have delivered your notes to the Registry, but that you received them back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And may I also take it that the parties have received copies of these notes? Yes. I see nodding on all sides. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, could you be given, please, the black exhibit binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Turn to tab 7, please. You were talking yesterday about the incident in Lisnja. We see at tab 7 a series of photographs. First of all, generally, what are -- what, as far as you understand it, do those photographs depict?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These photos were taken by an official of the public security station of Prnjavor after the disarmament, and they depict the trenches that the group of extremists had prepared for possible combat operations or whatever -- I'm sure they knew why they prepared them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the witness the original photographs or are we all working on black and white copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, if your original documents that you brought with you -- well, perhaps I could answer the question for you, Mr. Vasic, but I'd like you to agree, to make sure I am right about this. It's right that you brought copies of these photographs with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing I'm -- the only reason why I'm asking is if there are any colour copies or colour originals available, we could put them on the ELMO. If not, we'll have to deal with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are no coloured copies available, are there, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like you to confirm that, actually. Is that right, Mr. Vasic, you only brought black and white copies with you? I see you nodding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would say yes or no, because nodding --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- doesn't appear on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's take the very first page as an example. Perhaps you would put it on the ELMO, because I think it would help the interpreters. I'm just going to take this as an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Top or bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Top will be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you read what it says there, please, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A trench in the vicinity of the house of Puskar Zijad in the field towards Milosavci in Gornja Mravica. The trench is about five metres long. It is semicircular and it was constructed from dirt and the concrete blocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Lisnja at the time of this incident?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about this incident in the afternoon, by accident. I was on my way towards Prnjavor and I saw smoke. The first person I came across I asked what was going on. He told me that Lisnja was on fire. I got on a bus and then as I was driving through, I saw what was going on. I saw the situation after the disarmament and I saw that there were houses set on fire and that there had been shooting. There was real combat going on. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who was responsible from the authority's point of view? Who was in charge? Let me rephrase the question. Who was in charge of the attempt to seize these weapons from the inhabitants of Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that the authorities tried to reach an agreement about the hunting rifles and the Territorial Defence weapons, and I already mentioned the composition of the delegation that was involved in the negotiations. This attempt failed. Only some of the weapons were brought to the culture hall, but the group of extremists broke into the culture home and took the weapons away. In more specific terms, the operations were carried out by the public security station of Prnjavor, pursuant to the orders of their superiors from the security services centre in Banja Luka. And there was also a unit of Territorial Defence which cooperated with them in that operation, pursuant to the orders which we received from the army. In that unit, there were some 20 to 30 members of the so-called Wolves from Vucjak unit who were already at the time members of the 1st Krajina Corps of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll come to them in few minutes' time. But how long did the operation to secure these weapons take?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation took place in the afternoon, and on the following day until 11.00, there was nothing going on during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was anyone injured or killed on either side during the course of the operation?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a report was drafted on the operation, it was established that, among the people who were organised in the village, some four or six people had died. I can't remember exactly, but I'm sure you can find it in your documents. And one policeman was slightly wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was anyone prosecuted as a result of the incident or operation?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The complete documentation on the cases and on convictions can be found amongst your documents. All those who were involved in the operation were taken to task, but they did not -- they were not charged with armed rebellion, but rather for illegal possession of weapons and weapons smuggling. Also, five members of the Serbian ethnic group were convicted because they had sold those weapons in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think we'll find these details in tab 7. I'm, of course, very reliant on your help in this regard, Mr. Vasic. But perhaps you would direct the Chamber to the documents which show the conviction of those -- of the villagers and also of the Serbs who supplied the arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What -- I think what -- what I'm sure what the witness is doing, Your Honour, is he's taken something out of his briefcase. They are his original copies of the documents that we have in the binder. He may be a little bit more familiar with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you're able to look in the binder, Mr. Vasic, because they should all be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, everything should be under tab 7 in the binder. The --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not that one, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other one in the hands of Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Immediately after the photographs.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Immediately after the photographs, I can see an overview of criminal reports filed against certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Put those on the ELMO, if you would. Have a look first of all at what's on the screen. I'm certainly not going to ask you to read all of this out. Read -- it says 1992. Then read the four words after that, please.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "An overview of criminal reports filed."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do any of the names and details we see there relate to the incident in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost all of the data are relative to the incident in Lisnja. Only very few of them are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And are you able to cross-reference those entries with any other document as to what happened to those who were convicted of crimes in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Looking further on in tab 7, are you able to get more details of the crimes individuals were convicted of in relation to the incident which you've just been describing?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have this list of the criminal reports filed, as I've said, but afterwards we have references to the sentences passed by the court affairs instance in Prnjavor with reference to the same individuals, of course. And it can be seen that the criminal proceedings were conducted in line with all the relevant rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Take out of the bundle an example of that, please, and put it on the ELMO. I'd like you to read slowly the four words in the heading, and then all of number 1.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The court of first instance at Prnjavor. Number 1: The sentence of the basic court number K76/92, dated the 10th of November, 1992. Because of the crime of illegal detention of arms or explosives, according to Article 213, Para 1, taken over from the criminal law of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Time: By the end of 1991. Place: The village of Lisnja, in the municipality of Prnjavor. The damaged Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. party, nothing. Note: Prison sentence lasting two months and 25 days."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, take this person Mr. Osman as an example. As far as you know, did he ever serve that prison sentence?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody actually served a prison sentence. I believe the judge, especially if we look at all the other sentences, in the first few days, people were fined. They had financial penalties imposed on them. But as time went on, people were being given prison sentences that referred to the duration that they had spent in detention already, whilst waiting for their case to be heard. Here in this first case, it says 1991 and, in most other cases, 1992. Some individuals were sentenced because they were involved in the selling and buying of arms, even previously. It was an ongoing process for about six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before we move away from these documents, perhaps you could also help the Chamber. Immediately before this list, there is about ten pages between paragraphs 1 to 62, in Cyrillic script. Can you go to the first of those pages, please.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean just after the photos?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: After the photographs and after some other lists, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the only part in Cyrillic of the document.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If you'd put the first page on the ELMO. Read the heading in number 1, please.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Documents for Prnjavor. Number 1: The sentence for Osman Rahimic son of Ramadan, born on the 29th of May, 1952. Because by the end of 1991, in the village called Lisnja, in the municipality of Prnjavor, he obtained for free an M-48 rifle and 50 bullets from Husein Vukovic and he kept those items at home. And then, in April 1992, he exchanged the M-48 rifle for a semi-automatic rifle, and this exchange was entered into with Sead Korkaric and that was his partner in his duties as village guard. And then he relinquished those arms on the 17th of June, 1992 to the employees of the police station in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are a large number of lists in tab 7. Do they all relate to crimes committed by the inhabitants of Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There are also documents referring to crimes committed by five or six Serbs who actually sold those weapons to these other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you have a look at number 47, please, of that Cyrillic list. Could you read number 47 out.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The public security station in Prnjavor, a criminal report against Miroslav Simic, son of Milan, born on the 9th of June, 1958 in Derventski Lug, permanently resident at Derventa. Because on the 14th of August, 1992, in the village Ratkovac, in the municipality of Prnjavor, between 6.00 and 6.15 p.m., whilst travelling on a military vehicle TAM 110, he damaged a number of passenger vehicles which were parked in front of the Podgorica restaurant in Prnjavor. And then he continued his journey in the direction of Klasnice and he also ran into two cyclists and one of the two was injured. And the cyclists names are Grujic Dimitrije and Pezer Vesna.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I just want you to read one other example, and that's number 51, please.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could not receive English translation at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. The interpreter forgot to switch on the mic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you perhaps restart reading this paragraph. I think it was 51. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Public security station Prnjavor, certificate on temporarily taken items from Siljak Sladjan, son of Milan, born on 3rd of February, 1975 in Doboj in the municipality of Doboj, permanently a resident in Ceceva in the municipality of Teslic. Criminal report against eight individuals because in the night of the 27th of November, 1992, at around 10.30, they were in a group of both military and civilian individuals and they went to the Catholic church of Kulasi and they found four local men who were on duty in front of the church and they were told to sit on the benches in the church. And a part of the group that came along had gone to the parish, to the offices of the parish, which were not too far from the church. They broke into the office and there they found Anna Juric and a priest, Nikica Lozancic, who was questioned, mistreated, beaten, punched, and he was therefore injured. And they also ransacked the office. They smashed glass and crystal objects and then they also stole a TV set and recorder."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And can you confirm the individuals who were charged --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, but that seems to be an unnecessarily leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Number 52, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not -- excuse me, I'm caught down here. I'm not objecting to any pursuit -- information about this area; I simply want the information to come from the witness and not as a result of a statement presented by counsel. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 52, please. "Public security station Prnjavor. Criminal report against Mladen Kitanovic, son of Nikola, born on the 27th of August, 1945 in the village Bobare, the municipality Tesanj. Permanently resident in Babanovci in the municipality of Prnjavor. Because the said individual, on the 2nd of December, 1992, at around 6.30 p.m., after an argument and a fist fight that he had with Sefko correspond Totic in the yard of the house owned by Nikola Barkijevic from Babanovci. After that he went home to fetch a rifle in order to kill this other person. "Having collected a rifle from a room in his house, his family members tried to prevent him from taking it out of the house, but to no avail. He went to the above-mentioned courtyard and he was followed by his son, Dragan. When they got to the courtyard, Dragan tried to calm him down and to convince him to give up his intention. But on that occasion, his father first of all fired a bullet in the air from his rifle, M-48, and then he fired another bullet and he actually shot his son Dragan in the head. And therefore, on the way to the hospital, his son Dragan succumbed to the injury."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In number 52, the accused came from which ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these three criminal reports refer to the accused -- or rather, defendants who were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you say "three," which three are you referring to, for precision, please?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We read out numbers 51, 52, and 47. And 48 and 49 refer to murders where the accused individuals are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in number 52, the person whom the accused shot at originally, what ethnic group was he from?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person that he intended to kill was a Muslim, but his son, who was actually killed, is of course a Serb -- was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. There has been a witness who has given evidence to this Chamber, albeit by way of a 92 bis statement, that is, a statement that was read to the Chamber, who alleged that the judicial system in Prnjavor in 1992 was inherently unfair to Muslims. What do you say about that, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that it's incorrect, because all murders referred to here were adequately processed and documented and the people were sentenced. And in most cases - and that's a rarity even now - the perpetrators were discovered and sentenced, and some of them are still in prison today, after that many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like now to move on to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, could we perhaps ask the witness whether he could mention one or two of the persons still in prison for these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us just -- you said some of them are still in prison. Could you give us a few names of those still in prison.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I read out the name? Mladen Zgonjanin. He killed Ramiz Jugo. He was a Serb who killed a Muslim, and he was in prison and I'm pretty certain he was still in prison last year. I'm not sure if he's still there, but I do know that he served a long prison sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also, I'm not quite sure; I think later on he was transferred to a psychiatric hospital. It's number 49, Miodrag Debic, who killed a taxi-driver, Miljenko Beus, for financial gain. And he was in prison and later on we heard that he had mental health problems and was therefore transferred to a psychiatric hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I know we're struggling trying to cope with the absence of translations, but I think it's preferable if there's a reference to a particular passage of the document that we get some translation on the record. It's not going to cost us more -- it may cost us a little more court time, but it's going to have to be translated in any event for comprehensibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we'll ask, then, the witness to read the two examples he gave, the one being number 55. Could you please read 55. It looks as if a sentence of 20 years was imposed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Public security station, Prnjavor. Criminal report against Mladen Zgonjanin, son of Merko, born on the 27th of March, 1957 in Prijedor. Permanently resident in Prijedor because on the 13th of July, 1992, in the garden of the Nacional Hotel at Prnjavor, he wounded Ramiz Jugo from Prnjavor in the neck and after 20 days Jugo Ramiz succumbed to his injuries. Ramiz was in fact a member of the armed forces of the Republic of Srpska."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would you also read 49, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Public security station Prnjavor. Criminal report against Miodrag Debic, born on the 28th of July, 1965, because, on the 17th of May, 1992, at 5.00 p.m., he killed Miljenko Beus in a wood belonging to Rado Kesa."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the last example you gave, number 49, have you any idea of the ethnic origin of the victim and deceased in that case?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, the victim was a Croat. He was a taxi-driver in Prnjavor. That was his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to move on, please, to something you mentioned earlier, and that is the so-called Wolves from Vukjak. It's been alleged, again by at least one Prosecution witness, that they were a paramilitary outfit. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that a group of young men, I think about 18 of them, went for training to Knin and they received training from Captain Dragan. After a week, as we heard later, Veljko Milankovic - his name has been mentioned on a number of occasions - joined that group. Upon completion of that training, they returned to Prnjavor and we received information according to which they came back armed. There had been a number of difficult situations with the police, and on those occasions, those men had been disarmed. However, at that time, a conflict broke out in Western Slavonia, and that group, plus some volunteers, so that the group swelled to about 50 or 60 individuals, as I heard later, and under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps and following the orders from the corps commander, General Uzelac, they participated as a military formation in the fighting in Western Slavonia. And I believe they were in a unit which is called 309th unit, or something like that. Throughout the war, it was a regular military unit and the civilian authorities had no control over them. They gained fame in combat and quite a few of them were killed. Almost half of this total number of 300 at their peak were actually killed. They were killed because, as a unit, which later on depended on General Talic, who commanded the 1st Krajina Corps, were trying to break the lines on the front. And upon completion and every individual action they came back to base because they were never in charge of holding the front lines. And the base was on the territorial of the municipality of Prnjavor. In as far as the civilian authorities were concerned, it was a bit of a problem, because there were about a hundred -- rather, 1.500 soldiers, that is to say, one third of the total number of people mobilised in Prnjavor were always on the territory of the municipality, and they were all armed. Our MP, Dragan Djuric, tried to intervene with President Karadzic and tried to get him to reach an agreement with the armed forces on the basis of which soldiers going on home leave would have to leave their weapons at the barracks and come home unarmed. However, General Talic rejected that idea, and his rationale was that military men would not be safe if they were unarmed. You can only imagine how civilian authorities could function if at any given time there were 1.500 people walking around carrying arms and ammunition. However, all things considered, looking back, it wasn't as bad as it could have been, considering how many weapons there were in that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time. And I'm talking about a municipality such as Prnjavor, where there was no combat activity going on. The front line was about 30 kilometres away from the town of Prnjavor. I mean, the fact that General Talic actually had -- was in favour of the Wolves can be seen on the basis of special authorisations that they had, a number of prizes that they got. They had special authorisation to get weapons whenever and wherever they wanted. However, the fact is that they were a rather disciplined army. However, they did sometimes cause problems, because throughout the war, the army tried to meddle in civilian affairs. So we started protesting, saying that we couldn't do our job if they kept threatening us and saying that they would replace police officers or start arresting mayors, and that was something that happened quite often. So General Talic, following our insistence when all this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. culminated in September 1992, finally issued an order which is also included in one of the tabs here, and quite a few things transpired, quite clearly, from that order. He actually ordered for the military police in the municipality of Prnjavor to stop carrying out patrols of the round, that they could only carry out patrols in areas where combat activity was under way, and all police matters were to be taken care of by the police station of the municipality of Prnjavor. Also, he disbanded the Wolves from Vucjak unit. He then formed it again and issued an order for this unit to be sent and deployed in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look at the bundle, Mr. Vasic, at tab 5, please. What is tab 5?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was leaving to go to The Hague, I asked the association of veterans to give me a copy of the CV of one of the fighters that belonged to the Wolves from Vucjak unit, describing the time he spent during the war. And such CVs exist for every fighter from that unit. This is the CV of the deputy commander of the battalion, which clearly shows that throughout the war, they were members of military units of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Put it on the screen, because I think that might help all concerned. What is the name of the soldier whose record we see here?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miro Sikarac was this soldier's name. When commander Milankovic got killed, this person was appointed commander in his lieu. And earlier on, he was a member of the battalion, and you can see clearly in this document where he was and what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And -- yes. When you say "one can see clearly," read out slowly the parts that tell us where he was and what he did.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He joined the army on the 19th of September, 1991. He joined the Territorial Defence unit at the time. And he was in charge of providing security for various facilities. He remained in that position until the 28th of January, 1992, which is four months and ten days all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness first of all to point at the name on the ELMO on the list. I have still some difficulties in finding the name. Could you please, with the pointer, tell us where we find the name of the individual. Please, on the ELMO. Could you please -- no. I'd like you to watch what Madam Usher is showing you. Could you please turn to the right. Could you turn to your right and seek from the instructions of the usher to point at where the name appears on the document, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume this was on page 1, which I either didn't bring with me or it hasn't been photocopied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, perhaps during the next break you pay attention to -- because the -- what looks very much as a computerised record of activities --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is a computerised record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And where I also see that very often the same text reappears. So even for a translation, a couple of lines would already do and would make the remainder of most of the document understandable. But at least we have no name at this moment, so we can't relate it to any person.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask -- I'm going to move away from this topic. Could the witness give us, please, binder number 5 that he brought with him. One of those plastic binders that you've got, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Vasic find his own material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If you just give that to us, we will look at it and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be willing to give it to Mr. Josse so that he can have a look?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not find it necessary to photocopy those. I might have made a mistake. These are the records of some five or six thousand fighters, and I did not photocopy the name page, which obviously was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to apologise for it. Mr. Josse will have a look at it and see how he will proceed. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will ask you one other question about these lists in tab 5. What is your understanding as to the relationship between that list and the Wolves? When I say "that list," perhaps I should say that computer printout and the Wolves.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The link is as follows: In the list of all the fighters that were members of the Republika Srpska army, you can also find the record of the soldiers who were members of the Wolves, from Vucjak. That was only their popular name. People referred to them as Wolves, but otherwise they were members of those units. And my intention was to show you what units they were members of, because they were attached to some eight or nine different units, pursuant to the orders of General Talic. They were members of the 1st Assault Battalion and as such they were attached to various units. This is what their tasks were as volunteers. This was the only unit that was replenished from the ranks of volunteers. All the other units were replenished in the Secretariat for National Defence in different ways. They are the ones who themselves found volunteers and then they would go to the secretariat, asking the secretariat to assign them places in various units. General Talic personally sent them --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, because I think you've answered my question and I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, just for my understanding: From what we've seen at tab 5, I couldn't find a name. Is my understanding correct that this document is not about one person but gives records of many persons? For example, if I look at the fourth and the fifth entrants, I see as starting date in both cases 29th of January, 1992 -- or at least the first date. And the second date in both 17th of March, and at the same time, under 1 I see, well, at least Banja Luka as a place. And on the next one, which very much looks like Slavonia, whether it's Western Slavonia or not. So this is a compilation of many persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's our understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. This is the record of only one person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But how, then -- I pointed at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Many things were recorded. In the veterans association is as follows: Every case is recorded two times. Firstly, which unit they belonged to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And secondly, where their zone of their combat operations was. They also recorded the date of joining and the date of transfer to another unit. Every time one person was transferred, you will see this date being recorded in two different lines. I don't know why this was done like that. I can't tell you. In any case, what matters here is where you see the name of the war unit. This is what shows you clearly which unit a certain person belonged to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I then take it that one record takes approximately 12, 13 lines, so that we have approximately three records on the first page? Is that -- I'm just trying to understand what type of document I've got in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The best one can do, Your Honour, is ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking the witness whether we have three records on the first page, or do we have more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these pages belong to one soldier, unless there are double copies. Yes, I actually have double copies of each page. The record of this particular soldier consists of three pages. This is the case of which applies to the Wolves, who were -- very often changed units. All the other soldiers have records consisting of only one page, because they remained with the same unit throughout the war. But, as I've already told you, General Talic would assign them very often to different units. They would act as an assault battalion. They would be used to break through the enemy lines and then they would be sent home on leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So just to understand: This is about one man, and may I take it that the first 13 lines, then, cover the period of September 1991 until the 28th of January, 1992, when he was in the TO of Prnjavor, and that the next 13 lines cover the period of the 29th of January until the 17th of March, when he seems to be related to something in Banja Luka? utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It says the zone of combat operations, Western Slavonia, the war unit from Banja Luka, 8840. This is the designation or the number of the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we continue for the period of the 18th of March until the 31st of March, when he was again a member of the TO in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.text: And then the next is about the 1st of April until the 14th of May, when he was in Derventa, as far as I can see, a unit from Derventa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. 7127, Derventa.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was when the combat operations had already started in Derventa.

utterances.text: I've got now at least a global idea of what type of document is presented.

utterances.text: Yes. And then, Mr. Josse, the first three pages, the witness explained to us that this is a record of one person, three pages. utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to tell us what he knows about the origin of this group of men, the Wolves, and why were they given this name? Why did people refer to them as "the Wolves"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that most of them, if not all of them, were Serbs. The nucleus, when they returned from Knin and they were engaged in Slavonia, most of them were from the municipality of Prnjavor, Derventa, and partly from Doboj. Later on, they also received members from Banja Luka and other places. People volunteered to join them. So they were not territorially limited. They were all very young. I believe that some 70 per cent of them were not older than 19 or 20 at the time. They were renowned for their courage in combat operations. The commander, Milankovic, who joined them down there and imposed himself on the unit and became the commander of the unit, had been known to us before the war as a criminal. There were a lot of criminal reports against him for various crimes. However, during the war, he was wounded twice. He became a war hero and finally he got killed in combat. As a result of his courage and his skills, he was held in very high esteem by General Talic, the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't answer my question. Where does the name come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know. I never asked them, not even in informal conversations. I believe that somebody told them in Knin that they should call themselves something to be different from others. One of their characteristics was the fact that they did not wear any hats or caps. Whatever unit they were attached to, they always referred to themselves as the Wolves, although they were never a separate unit, a separate formation. This was their popular name that they had given themselves. And on one sleeve, they wore an insignia depicting a wolf's head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like now, Mr. Vasic, to turn to political --

utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Gaynor has arrived. If the Court had expressed an interest in the last few minutes, before Mr. Josse turns to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're at your disposal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, since it seems that you're moving to your next subject, perhaps it could wait and we could first hear what Mr. Gaynor wants to respond to the motions filed by the Defence, then have a break, and that we then start with your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps -- the witness doesn't have to -- we have to discuss, Mr. Vasic, a procedural issue which is still outstanding, which takes us a couple of minutes. We have a break after that. So there's no need for you to stay at this moment, so you could follow Madam Usher and we'd like to see you back most likely at approximately 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst the witness is leaving the court, Your Honour, could the Chamber inform me: Are the Defence entitled to an oral rejoinder of Mr. Gaynor's submissions? I ask because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends what he'll say. If he says that he fully agrees with the Defence, then of course there would be no need, but that's not apparently what you expect. Mr. Gaynor, let's first listen to him and then -- Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence has made three applications for certification. Two were filed on the 5th of October; one was filed on the 6th of October. I presume you wish me to respond in respect of all three. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever outstanding, we have to decide upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The Prosecution opposes all three Defence applications for certifications. In brief, our position is that the Defence has failed to meet the criteria set out in Rule 73(B) in order for the Trial Chamber to be in a position to exercise its discretion to grant certification, even if the criteria in Rule 73(B) are met, the Trial Chamber does retain a discretion to deny certification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's just try to be clear. Isn't it true that one of the motions is not for certification but is for an extension of time to seek certification?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It starts out that way. However, the motion goes on to actually seek such certification in paragraph 10, subparagraph 2, of that motion, the Defence actually seeks such certification. Now, in respect of the application for extension of time for that particular motion, the Defence has relied on a decision in the Blagojevic case, in which the Trial Chamber did make a suggestion that an appeal as of right lay in respect of decisions taken pursuant to Rule 98 bis. Now, there are considerable number of other decisions before the Trial Chamber and which certification was granted following decisions rendered pursuant to Rule 98 bis. Therefore, it was certainly open to the Defence to take the view that certification was still required under the new Rule. And there was really nothing in the new Rule which should have led the Defence to believe that an automatic right of appeal had suddenly come into existence where it did not exist before. Therefore, it may be that Your Honours wish to take the position that there is no good cause that's been shown by the Defence to grant the Defence an extension of time in order to apply for certification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's about the extension of time. Now about the certification as such. You say the Defence has not met the requirements of 73, I think it's B, but I have to look that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us in what respect the Defence has not met the requirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly. One by one. In relation to the Defence application for certification pursuant to Rule 73(B), to appeal against a decision on the motion for an extension of time. Here, essentially, the Defence is re-arguing the merits of its original application. Rule 73(B) is not intended to provide an avenue for re-arguing the merits. It's intended to provide for an appeal where the Trial Chamber has erred or may have erred on the matter of fact or of law. Now, the Defence suggests that the Trial Chamber unreasonably disregarded the shortage of time, resources available to the Defence. The decision shows that the Trial Chamber took due regard of the amount of time and resources available to the Defence throughout the totality of these proceedings. It acted within its discretion and no error in the exercise of that discretion has been shown. The Defence goes on to say that the Trial Chamber attached disproportionate weight to the question of the accused's obligations to contribute financially to his own defence and unduly penalised him, with the result that a fair trial has been unreasonably jeopardised. Our response to that is that the Trial Chamber in no way acted unreasonably. It took into account the Defence's own submissions that the accused has been very difficult with his own Defence team, to use the Defence -- Defence's own words. And it also took into account that the Defence itself has taken the position that the failure of the accused to present 180.000 dollars has had a significant detrimental effect on the presentation of Mr. Krajisnik's defence. Further, the Trial Chamber, in fixing the date of the 3rd of October, 2005, to commence the Defence case took into account submissions made by the Defence on the 23rd of August in which the Defence suggested that it might be ready on the 1st of October. Finally, in the Defence's -- in the Trial Chamber's decision, the Trial Chamber ordered the Defence to file in the most complete form possible, the list of witnesses. It did not require an exhaustive list of witnesses. It did not require the Defence to file its list of exhibits at that time. The order provided by the Trial Chamber built -- contained built into it a great deal of flexibility, and it's our position that no error in the exercise of the Trial Chamber's discretion has been shown in respect of that particular application. Now, in the application also filed on the 5th of October, entitled "Defence application for certification pursuant to Rule 73(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, to appeal against a decision on Defence motion to stay the proceedings," our position here is that an appeal on this would certainly not help to expedite these proceedings. In fact, appellate litigation on this issue would frustrate the expeditious conduct of the proceedings. The Defence have essentially asked the Trial Chamber to reconsider its decision not to hold in abeyance this trial while a possible Rule 98 bis appeal may go on. There is no general right for a trial to grind to a halt while an interlocutory appeal is taking place. The Trial Chamber has set out very clearly in its decision on the Defence motion to stay the proceedings, its understanding of how -- if an appeal were to be successful under Rule 98 bis, how it would deal with the evidence which had been presented by the Defence until that moment in time. There has been no error in the Trial Chamber's exercise of discretion in that decision either. On the decision of the 6th of October, 2005, this is the decision which in that motion -- this is the motion in which the Defence seeks an extension of time, pursuant to Rule 127, to apply for certification, and applies for certification are responded to the point on this application for an extension of time. In respect of the merits of the appeal itself, again, the Defence only made a very bare assertion in its Rule 98 bis submission concerning the whole of the indictment. Its detailed submissions were concerning really two points, first of all, whether there was any prejudice to the fundamental rights of the accused caused by the new Rule 98 bis; and second, whether the Prosecution had established -- had put forward evidence meeting the 98 bis threshold in respect of the genocide of the Bosnian Croats. Those were the two reasoned submissions for -- the Defence made. The Trial Chamber is not obliged to consider unreasoned submissions or any of bare assertions made by the Defence. It's only obliged to consider those reasoned decision made by the Defence. The Rule 98 bis decision itself considered the Defence's submissions in detail and no possible error of fact or law has been identified by the Defence. And for those reasons, we'd oppose that application also. Unless I can help you further, that ends our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we've heard the response by the Prosecution. Mr. Josse, would you like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can be very brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I in fact primarily deal with the request for the extension of time in order to certify the 98 bis. Because in my submission, that is an important matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would submit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd say, if there's no extension of time, you're too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There's no question about that. What I would submit is that in the -- this Chamber should ask itself first of all, in fact, whether it would in fact certify. The answer to that, despite what Mr. Gaynor said, must be yes. For a Chamber not to certify a 98 bis appeal would have to be extremely unusual. There were reasoned submissions. I accept what Mr. Gaynor said about some of the bold assertion that is were made, but there were reasoned submissions in relation to certain aspects of this indictment and in the normal course of events, the Defence submit this Chamber would certify. So far as the extension of time is concerned, there was a misunderstanding of the part of the Defence. It wasn't an unreasonable misunderstanding, we submit, bearing in mind the recent change in the Rules. The position is at the very best moot. The Appeals Chamber have now decided and have decided that one does still need to seek certification, notwithstanding the change of the Rules, but has shut the Defence out. As this Prosecution are now suggesting, let's make no bones about it, as they are now suggesting would be unfair in the extreme, bearing in mind the fact that it was an error in relation to what is, as I've already said, a rather moot new rule. So far as Mr. Gaynor's other submissions are concerned, could I say two things. First of all, he simply rehashes exactly what Mr. Tieger said. He addresses the merits of the various motions. He doesn't, in my submission, actually address the Rules in any very specific way. And finally this: Yet again, and I don't blame Mr. Gaynor for this because it was part of this Chamber's reasons for rejecting this particular motion, the matter of my client's financial contribution has been raised. It's a matter, as the Chamber is well aware, of the utmost sensitivity to Mr. Krajisnik and he's asked me to mention he simply doesn't accept what's been said in relation to that. I might put that on the record again. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. The Chamber will consider the matter and we will give decisions as soon as possible, possibly oral decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Krajisnik is concerned probably about the last thing that I said. Apparently he'd like to consult me on that issue. I will speak to him during this adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would speak to Mr. Krajisnik during the break, and if there would be anything to be added, you could do that immediately after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very kind of Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will adjourn until 5 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I would give you an opportunity to immediately address us after the break, once you had consulted with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make it clear that Mr. Krajisnik, and I speak very much on his behalf here, does not accept the assertion that he has failed to comply with his financial obligation. And what we submit is this: That the Chamber placed too much reliance on Mr. Krajisnik's alleged failure to make that financial contribution in relation to its decision not to grant more time. And the issue, the relationship between that financial contribution or lack of it and the granting of more time, or in fact in this case, not granting more time to the Defence, is one that should be considered on appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's perfectly clear, what you tell us. Before we continue, I would have one additional question. We're talking about three decisions, two filed on the 5th and one on the 6th of October. One of these requests for certification was later called a dead duck --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- by Mr. Stewart. That is the certification to appeal our decision not to grant a stay during the, at that time, appeal lying as of right. Meanwhile, the Appeals Chamber has decided that first application -- I mean, that's why we are dealing at this moment with some of the other ... The 6th of October submission, which asked for extension of time to apply for a certification to appeal against -- I mean, that's the result of the decision of the Appeals Chamber. And that certification to appeal our decision not to grant a stay is -- seems to be moot at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That, I think, is right, Your Honour. Because first of all, of course, this Chamber would have to grant the extension of time and the certification in relation to 98 bis. If it didn't do that, the stay would clearly be redundant. If this Chamber would grant the certification in relation to the 98 bis, as I understand it, and I don't pretend to be a huge expert on these rules, we then need to seek an extension of time from the Appeals Chamber, because we would be out of time so far as they're concerned. And it was only then I suppose if the Appeals Chamber granted us an extension of time could we ask for a stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about that, because it might be you have a limited time once the certification has been granted to file an appeal. So if we would grant an extension of time and if we would grant a certificate, then an the basis to certify the appeal, I think you would still have sufficient time. But whatever that may be, the 5th of October request for certification to appeal against our decision not to grant a stay was to grant a stay in respect of the appeal as had been filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think that matter is now closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if there would ever in the future be a moment where the Defence would consider again to ask for a stay or to -- then we'll see, but this one at least is resolved, I would say. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With respect, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we have two motions to decide upon in view of certificates. There's one other procedural matter I'd like to briefly raise. Again and again, we have not been struggling, but we at least have heard some evidence about majorities and minorities in terms of nationalities or ethnicities, but as far as I know, the 1990 census is not in evidence, which of course would give us the information very often now sought from witnesses. Could the parties agree that we would have the results of this census in evidence so that we don't have to revisit the matter again and again?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I thought the witness dealt with it orally at the beginning of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the next witness we'll have to do the same for his municipality and then for the next municipality we'll have to do it the same. If we once would have -- if the Chamber would call upon the parties to provide us with the results of the census, then we would all have it in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That seems very sensible, if I might say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if there would be any need to refer to it, of course, we could always do it. It's not to remain silent on majorities and minorities from that moment, but we don't have to establish what it was on the basis of the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would completely agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any party volunteering for -- I mean, we'd like to have this in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll be happy to volunteer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Josse, we'll ask Madam Usher to escorted the witness into the courtroom and then you'll have an opportunity to continue your examination-in-chief. At the end of this morning's session, I'll ask the registrar to attribute provisional exhibit numbers to the exhibits we've dealt with. Of course, we could not admit them until we have received the translation. Usually we wait for the translation before we admit any document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, please be seated. Mr. Josse, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like now to ask you, Mr. Vasic, about the destruction of religious buildings in Prnjavor in 1992. Briefly, could you list those religious buildings that were destroyed or attacked in your municipality in that time.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the municipality of Prnjavor, there were three Catholic churches. One was situated at Kulasi, one in Prnjavor itself, and one where the Italians lived in the village called Stivor. Already earlier on, when I was referring to those eight people who had been arrested, I mentioned that church at Kulasi, where the Catholic priest was beaten up. He then went to Zagreb. And the Italian church at the Stivor village, except for a single graffiti, had never been damaged. As to the other church at Kulasi, we had a meeting with the inhabitants of Croat nationality on the next day within the church itself. And then we had another meeting with the bishop Komarica in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, would you first focus on answering the question. Because you were not asked about meetings, you were not asked about where the priest went, but you were asked about destruction of places of worship, churches, mosques, whatever. Could you please focus on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think we'll move on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The church in Prnjavor -- well, there was an attempt to mine it. And two soldiers -- one soldier from Banja Luka and one from Celinac, were arrested and they had two bombs in their possession, tank bombs. And they were questioned, and after questioning, they were escorted by police officers to the prosecutor's office in Banja Luka. And so the church was not mined, and even today there is no damage to speak of there. There was a single graffiti. It said "Seselj." And a week ago, the facade of this church was re-painted and so even that single graffiti has now disappeared. So those two churches were not destroyed. Ukrainian minority church at Prnjavor was destroyed. There were two Ukrainian churches, one Catholic, or rather, the Unionist and an Orthodox church. So the Ukrainian Unionist church was not destroyed, and the Ukrainian Orthodox church was. A couple of days before this attempt at destroying the Catholic church in Prnjavor, during questioning at the police station, one woman recognised one of the arrested individuals and she said that she did see him next to the Ukrainian Orthodox church. We were of the view --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you and ask you to move on, because you've dealt there with the various churches.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To mosques, please.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque in the village of Lisnja and Poraci, that's a single village, in fact. It is a part of the village of Lisnja which is called Poraci and there were two mosques there. In the aforementioned action, both mosques were destroyed. In the same way, later on when we saw the reports, we learned that shots were being fired from the mosques and that there was an arms warehouse in the mosque. I don't know whether this is correct or not. The Prnjavor mosque was destroyed and the criminal report was filed against unknown perpetrators. A mosque in Konjuhovci was destroyed in 1994 and a suspect was brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, because we don't need to examine 1994 at this stage. Have a look, please, at tab 9 of the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you ask the witness to do so, could the witness please explain when he said that shots were fired from the mosque and that the mosque in Lisnja was destroyed during the action. How was it destroyed? I mean, you can mine a mosque, you can take hammers and take out the basement. What -- in what way was the mosque destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said -- I just heard from the police and the people involved in that action, but I myself was not an eyewitness to anything. I heard those rumours about the Poraci mosque, but I had arrived and I was standing together with the Muslim president Ramo Seperovic when two soldiers came along and said that the mosque was on fire. They asked what they should do, and I turned round and I looked and saw a shop and I saw two fire extinguishers there and I said, "Break the glass and get these fire extinguishers and try to put out the fire." That's what they did, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is not an answer to my question. I mean, a mosque can be on fire because of arson, a mosque can be on fire because it was hit by any grenade or mortar fire. What do you know what destroyed the mosque? Because just fire just often --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that detail. I'm not aware of that detail. All I know is that the president of the village, a Muslim, can probably tell you, because he was standing next to me and he can testify to the fact that an attempt was made to put the fire out. But I don't know how it was set on fire. I wasn't even allowed to go there, because I was a civilian. I was standing there with the president of the village, at a distance of about 500 metres, 500 metres away from the events that were taking place at the end of that action. Because I got there rather late as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The mosque and the minaret, were they of bricks or of wood? What was the construction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The upper part was made of wood, and there was quite a bit of wood there, in fact. And other than that, it was a brick building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The minaret?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The minaret was made out of wood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was made out of wood. Was it still standing when you saw it or was it already -- I mean, was the construction still there or was it just the remains?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those two guys came back after a while and they said that they couldn't put it out because it was made of timber and that fire had caught everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The young men in question were Sinisa Gataric and another one called Ricko. They're the two people who tried to put the fire out. They were members of the police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look at tab number 9, please, Mr. Vasic. First document in that tab, the one in Cyrillic, please put it on the ELMO, because I'm going to ask you to read this. If you'd read it out, then I'll ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prnjavor, on the 14th meeting held on the 23rd of June, 1992, looking into the request of the Main Staff of the Islamic religious community of Prnjavor relating the security of religious buildings in Galipoljice and Konjuhovci reached the following conclusion: The Crisis Staff is in favour with providing security with regard to the religious buildings of the Islamic religious community in these places and for that to be done on the part of the police officers of the police station in Prnjavor. "As to the price for that and number of people needed, this is the information -- the facts that will be established at a later stage, together with representatives of the Islamic religious community in Prnjavor."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And dealing with the right hand bottom corner, there's a stamp. What is that stamp?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the stamp of the municipality of Prnjavor and my signature as president of the Crisis Staff in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does it have your name there in Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says Nemanja Vasic, a graduate in economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about in the left-hand corner, opposite that, where it says 1, 2, 3? Would you read out the heading and 1, 2, 3, please.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "To be delivered to the public security station in Prnjavor." That's number 1. Number 2: "The main council of the Islamic community in Prnjavor." And number 3 is the files of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We haven't dealt with the Crisis Staff, but you've just told us you were the president of it. We might come back to that a bit later. But why did the Crisis Staff make this promulgation?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff passed this decision for two reasons. The first one was the fact that a request had been made by the Islamic community for us to do that. And the second one was the fact that there were fears that something like that might happen because the rate of crime was on the rise, the crimes could not be curbed. There were lots of people with weapons roaming around the town and the police station had a very difficult time coping with all that. Basically, this was a measure of prevention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Turn to the second document, please, in this particular folder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, one thing is not entirely clear in relation to this document. When read out, it says that the price has to be set at a later stage. What do I have to understand by "the price"? Was this just a matter of calculation for what it would cost the municipality of Prnjavor or would they have to pay for -- would the Islamic community have to pay for these measures of protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the police station had its superiors along the vertical line, we could only issue conclusions, but not orders. Or we could agree with some orders, if some costs were accrued. There was room for the Islamic community and the public security station to reach an agreement. In this particular case, there was no compensation, nothing was paid for the services. This was just a way of preventing somebody coming up with an excuse, and the excuse being additional cost. That's why this clause was included into the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The second document in this tab is from a bishop, as we can see. Am I right? I'm sure I can lead on this. He was the Catholic bishop of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And if you would read -- the letter is to a Mr. Vincic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I started telling you about that. After the events in Kolasanin [phoen], after the group that had attacked the priest had been arrested, I made an arrangement with the bishop in Banja Luka for the transport of the priest from Prnjavor to be secured so that he could hold services in Kolasija [phoen]. And you can see what was done and then -- I'll start reading it now, as a matter of fact. "The Mr. Vincic, the chief of the public security station of Prnjavor. "Dear Sir, I have been informed about your attempts to preserve the necessary peace and order in these hard times in the area of your competence. I'm also familiar with your attempts to provide our parishioners to follow religious services. For a while now, one of the police officers of your police station has been escorting the priest, who goes to the church in Kulasi to perform religious services there. I would like to express my gratitude for all your help. In these hard times, people like you are very precious, because they appreciate that there can be no real state without the rule of law, which provides guarantees for the human rights to every person, to every religious or ethnic community. I am convinced that you will continue pursuing this. I would like to thank you once again. I remain your sincerely Franjo Komarica, the bishop of Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, because I think that speaks for itself. Could we move on to the issue of population movements, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about, firstly - and listen to my question carefully, Mr. Vasic - problems that the civilian authorities in Prnjavor faced in 1991 and 1992 in relation to Serb refugees.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of combat operations in Western Slavonia, 9.000 refugees of Serbian ethnic background arrived in the municipality of Prnjavor. All those refugees were accommodated, in 99 per cent of the cases, in the Serbian houses. In my house, I had nine refugees for a year and a half. Since this was just the beginning of conflict in Croatia, in Bosnia there was still no war, and in economic terms, they did not pose too much problem for us, because the population in Prnjavor still had plenty of food and funds to provide for that population. And the municipality itself also had ample funds to assist them with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd now like to move on to the departure of Muslims from Prnjavor in, firstly, 1991, 1992. Were there any departures, and if so, when and why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we ask the witness, just for my better understanding of his previous answer, the beginning of combat operations in Western Slavonia. When in time was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was when the conflict in Croatia started. I believe we're talking about 1991, as early as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any more specific time of the year, spring, summer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it was the autumn of 1991, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question I asked a moment ago. Were there any departures of Muslims from the Prnjavor municipality in 1991 and 1992, and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me one sentence about something that is important with regard to that question. Before the war, there were about 7.000 people working in Austria, Germany, and Switzerland from the municipality of Prnjavor. Out of those, some 1.500 were Muslims. And when it looked like the conflict from Croatia would spill over to Bosnia and Herzegovina, all these people who worked abroad tried to bring their wives and children away from Bosnia and Herzegovina and bring them over to them, where they worked. That's why in 1991 and 1992, that is immediately before the conflict, most of the people left Prnjavor. The next wave was in 1995. According to our estimates, about 2.000 Serbs and about 1.000 to 1.500 Muslims all together left during that period of time. They were just afraid of a war, and also some others left if they could obtain either work permits or visas to go to other countries. At that time, when this was being done, there was still no conflict and they could not seek asylum.
