The main characteristics of departures that took place early on was the fact that they had members of family already living abroad and that's how they could obtain visas to move out to third countries. And the main reason why they did that was their fear of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There have been allegations in this courtroom in relation to your municipality that Muslims had to pay for the privilege of leaving. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The executive board of the municipality of Prnjavor could issue decrees or orders stipulating the conditions of departure. They had to settle their bills, first of all. Because these departures took place before the conflict. So this applied to everybody across the board, to the Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. All of them had to settle their debts, pursuant to some orders that the executive board could issue. And I know that it was said in the courtroom here that some people had to pay for their departure, but that happened later on, when those people were transported via the corridor through Serbia and Hungary, by private companies from Germany and Austria. There was still traffic for as long as there was corridor, there was traffic through that corridor. And I don't exclude the possibility that they had to pay either to the drivers or the organisers of those journeys for their illegal passage. But I only heard rumours of that. I was never officially informed of any such thing happening. I'm talking about the period 1991, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: After the exodus that you have just described, were any Muslims left in Prnjavor for the duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our estimates, some 1.500 Muslims remained there throughout the war. We don't have any official records of that. I believe that Merhamet will have that, Merhamet is the only organisation that functioned as of September 1992 as the organisation of the Muslim people in the municipality of Prnjavor. And later on, from mid-1991 to the end of the war, in case people wanted to leave, this organisation cooperated with the Red Cross and they drafted lists, they delivered them to the Red Cross, they provided for escorts and things like that. But up to 1995, I believe that not more than 1.000 people left, in smaller groups, and they ended up in the countries of western Europe. Very few of them ended up in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Those that remained throughout the war, in your estimation, as president of the Municipal Assembly, were they persecuted?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who remained, in my view, were not persecuted. But they suffered maybe a bit more than the Serbs, because there were fewer of them. There were various problems, and all of those were an integral part of the war. In case they wanted to move about, they were issued with the same permits as the Serbs. And those permits were to assist them. If anybody had been caught without a permit on any of the roads there, there were a lot of checkpoints, military checkpoints, where the military stopped vehicles, would not allow passage to anybody who did not have a permit of that kind. They were not terrorised in the sense of being sacked from their jobs, like some witnesses claimed here, but they had to obey rules, they had to act in keeping with the regulations, just like anybody else, Serbs or any other people. In your documents, you can see a list of people who were issued with permits to move about, and you can see that there is a lot more Serbs than Muslims there. And as for people being fired, could you please show the Chamber a decision that I signed on behalf of the Municipal Assembly. This decision was issued on the 11th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've referred, Mr. Vasic, to two different documents. First of all, if we go to tab 8, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, could we ask from the witness where he said the Muslims suffered more because there were fewer, which is not immediately understood by me. In what way did they suffer more, a bit more, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is only logical. If 1.500 Serbian soldiers move around the town with weapons, then Muslims would fear more than the Serbs if put in the same situation of having to walk through the same streets. And also there were some night visits and intimidation, and it happened more to the Muslims than to the Serbs. And it can also be seen from the documents that you have what measures were being put in place to prevent those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's first of all -- I don't think we do need to put it on the ELMO, actually. Take tab 8, please, in front of you. It's clearly a list. It's a handwritten list. Well, it has been put on the ELMO. That's fine. What is this, Mr. -- in fact, could we go to the second page, which is 1992, please, because it's a little more relevant. What is this?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list of people who were issued with a permit to leave, either to go abroad, to Banja Luka, to Belgrade. So these are issues to move outside of the municipality of Prnjavor. If somebody wanted to move about the municipality of Prnjavor, they didn't have to be issued with any special permit. These are several different lists pertaining to different years, to different days. We had many such lists, because a lot of people applied for a permit to move out or to go out of the municipality on any given day. And looking at the names, you can tell what the nationality of these people were. In this particular list that is now on the ELMO, under number 838, you can see Nevzeta Dervic, a Muslim lady from Prnjavor. The next on the list is Gordana Tomas, a Serbian lady from Prnjavor. The next one is Milica Dopudj, also a Serbian lady. Biserka Dopudj, another Serbian lady. This is not legible. The family name is Avdic. The father's name is Muhamed, and this means that the person is Muslim. Then Gordana Mihajlovic, a Serbian lady. Tomo Korjanic, a Serb under 845. Under 846, Stojan Marjanovic, a Serbian. Nada Bardak, 847, a Serbian lady. 848, Dusan Korjanic, a Serb. 849, Meho Pandzo, a Muslim. 850, Mahmut Mesic, a Muslim. 851, Boska Kitic Ilija, a Serb. 852, Stefano Fedlesic, Italian.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you, because for my purposes, we get the idea. And so who would have made these entries in these particular ledgers that the municipality kept? In other words, who was the record-maker?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This record was kept by the official who was in charge of issuing permits to all the citizens who applied for one and who were entitled to be issued with one. And everybody was entitled to being issued with a permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we now turn to tab 4, please. And in tab 4, I hope somewhere near the front, is a document in Cyrillic, but on the first line has the date the 11th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be put on the ELMO so that we can all see what we're talking about. It looks as if it's the first page under tab 4. Is that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Before you read this out, just tell us what it is, because it may not all be relevant.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decision on measures being taken with regard to the complex political and security situation in the territory of the municipality of Prnjavor. This was issued by the Municipal Assembly of Prnjavor on the 11th of October, 1991, when this was the time when the municipality was still functioning, all the MPs were there, the assembly was being convened and all the parties had their seats in the Municipal Assembly, the SDS and all the other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's number 3 that I want you to read out, please.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It is ordered to the company managers that on 15 October 1991 they send an official for national defence or any other responsible person to the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence, in order to define a list of conscripts who will be issued a mobilisation call to the war units or Territorial Defence, or the list of conscripts who have responded to those calls and who have not responded to that call. All those who have not responded to the call without reason and who have failed to turn out for work within the stipulated deadline should be issued a decision on their jobs being terminated."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what does that mean, please?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that all those who have been called to join the army did not have to come to work. A lot of witnesses have said that if they didn't join the army, that they were fired. One has to pay special attention to the part of the sentence which reads: "If they failed to respond to the call for mobilisation without a reason," and I emphasise, "Who have failed to turn up for work within the stipulated deadline provided for by the law, these people should be issued with a decision on the termination of their job." This means that those who didn't want to join the army had to continue coming to work. Under the law on labour relations that was in effect at the time, if you failed to turn up for work for three days without any justified reason, you would lose your job. The motive for this decision had more to do with the Serbs than anybody else. The military wanted to have a clear record of those who failed to respond to the mobilisation call. They were deserters in their book and they could easily be found at work if they indeed continued working. That's why people did not turn up for work, in order not to be found by the military. And we were responsible for the companies functioning properly. A lot of workers had been mobilised and a lot of them had failed to turn up for work, and the companies still had to operate, and we were in charge of supervising that. If somebody was fired, that doesn't mean that they were fired because they had failed to respond to the mobilisation call, but because they had failed to turn up for work. And this is clear from this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like to turn your attention to tab 10, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in order to avoid whatever misunderstanding: So you tell us that they were fired for not showing up at work. But if they did not follow the --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least that then they could be fired if they would not appear at their jobs. And that if they did not follow the -- if they had not responded to the mobilisation call, that they were at risk to be found by the military if they would be on their jobs. Being deserters, they could be easily found there. And did I understand you well that for that reason they might not have shown up at work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously, there's a misunderstanding here, or maybe I didn't make myself clear. It says here that the company managers were being ordered to send national defence advisor or somebody else in charge of those matters because it needed to be established what the situation was, and they had to act in line with the law. I didn't say that they would be dismissed automatically. I just explained that there were certain cases, but you can't see that directly on the basis of this particular article of the decision. But the main aim was to have a full record of all the people. That was the order we had received to help with the mobilisation process. And one form of such assistance would be this: According to the previous system that applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina, every company had one employee who was in charge of, generally speaking, national defence issues. So it was simply in order to establish how many people responded to this mobilisation call, who didn't -- who did so for justified reasons, who did so for unjustified reasons, and therefore, if those reasons were found to be unjustified, the people in question would be dismissed. That was just a set of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. instructions for company directors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that. But apart from the decision itself, you explained to us, and I just wanted to verify whether I correctly understood it, that those who without any valid reasons failed to respond to the mobilisation call, that those were considered - and I'm now using your own words - "deserters, and that they could be easily found at work if they indeed continued working. That's why people did not turn up for work." And as a consequence for not turning up for work, you could be fired. Is that -- I'm just trying to see the logic in your answer and to see whether I fully understood it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've tried to explain the fact that we had to have complete records, because the people at the company might have thought that a certain employee was at war. And the military thought that the person was at work. It would have been a bit confusing. We had to establish where everybody was. And perhaps they had the impression that if they were in a certain place, the reason given would be unjustified reasons, et cetera, I probably would have had the same impression had I been in their place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but apart from having good records to know exactly what happened, I can imagine that a factory would like to know whether one of their workers was absent because he went -- he responded to the mobilisation call or whether he would be absent for any other reason. I fully understand that. But this in fact resulted in those who did not respond to the mobilisation call were at risk, as you explained to us, when they went back to their jobs, because they could be found there, and while not showing up at their jobs, they were at a risk of being fired, having no good reason not to be on their jobs. Is that a correct understanding of what happened? I fully understand that those responsible both for factories and for the military would like to have a clear insight in who was supposed to be where, but is this what then actually happened for those who, without a good reason, did not respond to the mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right. But we are referring to the decision dated the 11th of October, 1991. So at that stage, there was no immediate threat of war. There was no state of war, as it were. According to the Territorial Defence law, everybody is obliged to respond to such a mobilisation call. It was a kind of mobilisation which was tantamount to an exercise of sorts, because we have seen at what point there was some preparatory work for combat activities, and it was actually in the spring after that. And this is much before that. It has nothing to do with the actual war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to law, they were obliged to respond to this mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Those who responded to the mobilisation call, was there any chance that they would be sent to Croatia, where there was a war at that time, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a single unit from Prnjavor in Croatia, and that was all, and it was a platoon, and they were mobilised much, much earlier. And they went there, and they were indeed there, as well as the before mentioned Wolves who were attached to some Banja Luka unit, according to the orders of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other units were simply being formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 10, please. You mentioned a little time ago the charity Merhamet. This is a document from them. I'd like you to read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The meeting of MHD" - I really don't know what it is - "Merhamet Prnjavor with representatives of the UNHCR. Point 1: Meeting the new deputy of the office of UNHCR based at Banja Luka. And point 2: The transfer of inhabitants who would like to leave this area across the Davor crossing. The response from the UNHCR was that the Croatian authorities did not express any wish to receive and accept any Muslim refugees from this area." And a question put by the UNHCR representative to the president of the Merhamet as to whether the Muslim population was driven out of their homes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one quick question. I didn't quite understand what the witness was referring to when he said, "I really don't know what it is." I don't know if that means he's referring to some particular aspect of this document or the document in general. If the latter, it seems to me there is something of a foundation issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant was this acronym just before the word "Merhamet." It is probably Muslim, M for Muslim, and D for Drustvo, which is an association, and I don't know what the H stands for. So it is a kind of acronym -- or no, no, no. I've just remembered. The Muslim Humanitarian Society, Merhamet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems, Mr. Tieger, that the witness wasn't sure about the abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As one, again, minor clarification, I note that the heading indicating the place and date was omitted. I think that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would read as Prnjavor, the 30th of October, 1995. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse. Perhaps you could invite the witness to continue reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think you had got to Odgovor, the paragraph beginning Odgovor or something approximating that. Apparently not, I'm told by -- wherever you'd got to, just continue.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had got to item 2. "The question put by the UNHCR representative to the president of the MHD. Has the Muslim population been driven out of their homes and taken to the sports stadium at Prnjavor?" And the answer from the president was the following: "That information is incorrect." And such cases have never taken place in the course of the war. And he went on to add that he could confirm that "the truth is quite different and what I want to say is this: Muslims in Prnjavor have never experienced anything of the sort and have always enjoyed the protection from the authorities in Prnjavor to the extent that it was possible at that time. The protection refers to the protection of personal property and human life, and I claim upon my own responsibility that in the course of the war, there were no rapes of Muslim women and there was no driving people out of their homes by force. And in the last days of war, the War Presidency of the municipality of Prnjavor prevented an exodus taking place in Prnjavor or anything along those lines. Because of the fact that the Presidency took the side of the people and left it up to them to make their own decisions as to whether they wanted to stay or leave this area. I would like to stress that I would like for this information to be forwarded to Geneva, because at any time I am in a position to confirm that this is indeed the truth and that on the territory of the municipality of Prnjavor, no distinction is made in terms of protecting people on the basis of their ethnic group." And that is addressed to the president of the municipality of Prnjavor, the chief of police, and the UNHCR office in Banja Luka and the Muslim humanitarian society Merhamet, in Prnjavor. The president of the Muslim humanitarian society Merhamet Prnjavor, Turin Sakib, Prnjavor, the 30th of October, 1995." I would just like to stress that no representative of the municipal authorities was present at that meeting. It was a meeting between the Merhamet representatives and the representatives of the UNHCR from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And further to that, how did you get hold of this document?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that was forwarded to us through official channels back then, and afterwards I photocopied it in order to have it as evidence, because as soon as a statement was taken from me, I supposed I might be invited as a witness before this Tribunal, and I thought that this document might be of some use in order to give a proper overview of the situation in the municipality of Prnjavor at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, in my remaining time, I want to turn to the Municipal Assembly, the executive committee, and the Crisis Staff. The Municipal Assembly, of which you were president, did that continue to operate through 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly and the Executive Committee of the municipality of Prnjavor were functioning in 1991 and 1992. Since the decision on the setting up of the crisis staffs gave us the opportunity to allow these bodies to continue to function in those places where they could and in those places where it was more difficult --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, because I'd like you to try and answer the question, if you could, please. I want to deal with each in turn. The Municipal Assembly, did that continue to function through 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Executive Committee, did that continue to function as well?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you have any part in the Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never participated in any meetings of the Executive Committee. I didn't deem it necessary. And according to the League of Professions, it wasn't within my duties to do so. But I've often talked to the president of the Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the Municipal Assembly is concerned, did the representation in that body change at all during 1991, 1992? In other words, did its ethnic composition change?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were changes, because according to the League of Professions, those who are elected officials can't be members of the Municipal Assembly. But according to the same election law, their places would be taken by other names on the same list of the same party. There were other changes as well. By the end of 1992, I think two people were replaced because they had been killed and, for that reason, others had to take their places.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we look at tab 11, please. Again I'm sure I can lead to this degree. This is a register of the names of the members of the Municipal Assembly at the relevant time and a register of their attendance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Again, very briefly, if you'd help the Chamber with the symbols. What does a 0, or an "o" represent?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "O" means that someone is absent for a justified reason,"+" that they attended the meeting and,"-", they were absent for unjustified reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's right that the vast majority of members of the Municipal Assembly in Prnjavor were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you help us with the Muslim members of the assembly. Take us to their names by reference to the number against their names, please.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims had six councillors, I believe, from the SDA party. And SDP, or the communists, that is, they had 11 councillors and there were a couple of Muslims among them as well. As to the names, Husein Vukovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Number, please.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just move this up a bit. Number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I actually think it would help if you had the document in front of you. You can put mine on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's okay like this. Then Klokic, Fuad, number 23, Ahmet Klokic, number 24. Could you just move it up a little more? And then Nusret Pandza, number 29. Mujo Rahimovic, number 42. Curan -- I can't read this, really. It's number 50 -- 52, sorry. And Ago Cehic, number 55. Mehmed Sabic, number 56. And another Sabic. I think -- I can't really read this, but it's 57. And then Ramadan Seperovic, number 58. So these were the Muslim councillors.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Many of those names have been scored through. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the witness answers this question, I have some difficulties. I might have missed something, but on the transcript, I read, as far as the "Os" or the "0s" are explained to the witness, the answer was: "'O' means that someone is absent for a justified reason, that they were absent for unjustified reasons." Which is quite confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What the witness said was"+" was for justified reasons. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said that"+" was for people who were present, who actually attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "+" is for presence. Zero is for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zero, absent for justified reasons. And "-", absent for unjustified reasons. Perhaps there was a justified reason, but the practice was if we didn't know of the reason, we would put a "-".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the "-" is absent for either unknown or unjustified reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Many, but not all, of the Muslim names that you have just read out have been scored through. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a notebook, a record kept by one of the employees, and I think it was the secretary. And some names are underscored, others are scored through, both Serb and Muslim names, and I can't see that there is a rule or a system here. So I'm not in a position to give you a proper answer. Perhaps in some cases he wanted to underscore the name and then he scored it through, in fact. And in other instances he was maybe writing other things down, making annotations or whatever. But there is no rule either with reference to Serbs or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And finally on this document, are there any -- were there any Croatian representatives on the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment. There was someone. Just a second. I think it would be a bit easier if I could take a proper look at the list. Number 34, Zarko Maric, a Croat. Apart from that, HDZ did not participate Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in the elections there, so it was an SDP councillor who was a Croat in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there was also Branislav Vukojevic, number 7. I think he was an SDP councillor as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put that down now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to move on briefly, I hope, to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you're looking at the clock at the same time. Could you give us an estimate on how much time you would need at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am as determined as I can be to leave the Prosecution some time today to begin their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is not in a position to begin today. We're still awaiting the translation of certain documents, we're still awaiting a response from inquiries we made in reaction to receipt of some of these documents. There was, as I think the Court can see, only a small fraction of the documents actually referred to in Court that were translated which we must review more carefully. As a result, in addition to actions we took in response to the receipt of notification about this witness, which was already a compressed time period, and then the belated receipt of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We often have put questions to the Defence not whether they were ready to cross-examine but whether they were ready to start to cross-examine the witness. I do take it that some time, limited time, is left. Could you try to find at least some portion of the cross-examination which you could start today, not expecting that you are fully prepared, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand the Court's point, of course, Your Honour, and of course I will look carefully at the material and do my best to comply with the Court's request. I will say, however, that it may well be the case that I will return and tell the Court that I think it really is necessary to have the information that we are currently awaiting in order to know how to frame any portion of the examination. I hope that's not the case, but I want to foreshadow that it may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see what you could do. We'll then adjourn now until 5 minutes to 1.00. So we would then have 50 minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is not in. Then please could you escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst he's being brought in, I used virtually the whole of the adjournment to confer with my client, and he's asked me to ask some questions. I have no disagreement about those questions. It's really a matter of emphasis, bearing in mind the available time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will see how I get on, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But so your consultation has led to a situation in which you put the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I didn't ask Mr. Krajisnik that question in terms. I suspect he'd like to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- how I do it. I'm going to ask what he's asked me to ask. Whether I ask it in a sufficiently thorough way to his satisfaction, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then see whether there's need for one or two additional questions. But this is exactly the course the Chamber would like to be followed. Mr. Vasic, please be seated. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you, I've already said, about the Crisis Staff. Short questions, and if you can, Mr. Vasic, in short answers: When was the Crisis Staff set up in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the decision of the Presidency of the Republic and the instruction of the government of the Republic, the Crisis Staff was set up in May 2002 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 1992, I assume. Yes, 1992. I apologise. It was on the 15th or on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For how long did it last? In other words, when did it cease to exist?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was disbanded at the session of the Municipal Assembly, when all the decisions of the Crisis Staff were adopted. This was in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And during the time it existed, to whom did it report?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in Prnjavor was very specific. The Presidency and the government suggested that wherever there were conditions for the functioning of the Municipal Assemblies, they could continue operating. So throughout all this time, when the Crisis Staff was in place, the executive board of the Municipal Assembly existed, adopted decision, and its decisions were also adopted at the same session of the assembly, at which the decisions of the Crisis Staff were adopted. It reported to the assembly, and the first session of the assembly was held in August, as I've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about minutes or reports? Were they sent --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Minutes or report, were they sent to anyone or any body outside of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The minutes were adopted at the assembly session and all the minutes were presented to the MPs. I don't remember whether we had that obligation and whether we informed the so-called government of the autonomous region of Krajina, or whatever its name was at the time. The Crisis Staff of Krajina, whether we informed them or not, I don't think we did. Sometimes we would send them a request. I don't think that we were even under obligation to report to them or to send them information, but I can't be sure of that. I don't know this for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To what extent, if at all, would you say the Crisis Staff was controlled either from Sarajevo or from Pale?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this period, the communication lines were bad, there was no corridor, and we were left to our own devices, more or less. And during that period, we only had some contacts with the AR Krajina. Before and after that period, we made fun of this AR Krajina. We did not consider it a factor, to be honest. But let me be more specific. During that period of time, from the moment the Crisis Staff was set up to the moment its decision adopted by the assembly, we did everything on our own and we were responsible for whatever was done in Prnjavor. The only cooperation we had with the bodies that had their superiors in Banja Luka, but this cooperation was just coordination, because there was no line of subordination. For example, the police had its regional office in Banja Luka and they were subordinated to them. They would send them requests and these requests could be met with only if an order to that effect was issued from their superiors in Banja Luka. I am talking about the Territorial Defence, about the civilian police. The vertical line of command went to their respective offices in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to seek a clarification from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your testimony you have indicated that the minutes were adopted at the assembly sessions and all the minutes were presented to the MPs. Could you be more precise in that respect, especially when you said that they were presented to the MPs. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a legal obligation for all the decisions of the Crisis Staff to be offered for adoption to the assemblymen of the Municipal Assembly as soon as the conditions were in place for the session to be called. I believe that we had that possibility before anybody else, because in the territory of our municipality there were no war operations. The only problem was that a lot of assemblymen were in the front lines, and that's why we had the problem of quorum. And that's why the assembly was not called that often. In lieu of that, we had Crisis Staff sessions. The first assembly session was called on the 14th of August, and all the decisions of the Crisis Staff were adopted at that session. That's what I meant. And this was the last session of the assembly in a mixed composition. When I say that, I'm referring to the Muslims, the Croats stayed until the very end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to show you next, please, Exhibit 65, tab 66, a document that this Chamber is very familiar with. The Registry have very handily produced the original exhibit. I do have some copies, but I don't think it will be necessary. This is a document that we all know as variant A and B. When was the first time, Mr. Vasic, that you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document the first time when you showed it to me here, and that was also the first time I heard of the document, when I first came to give my testimony here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just follow that up by asking you this: Did you attend, at the end of 1991, any meetings at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was a meeting of the Main Board, and I was not a member of the Main Board. However, the presidents of the municipalities were called to attend the meetings of the Main Board. I and the president of the Executive Board and the secretary of the assembly were in Sarajevo, and I was in the meeting in Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you were at the meeting at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo? Do you know the date? If you don't, say so.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was either in the autumn or in the winter of 1991. I can't remember exactly. In any case, it was late, in late 1991. I can see the date on this document. I suppose it is related to that event, but I cannot be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, you worked out my question may be related. All right. We can move on. I want to next ask you about something called the six strategic goals. What is your awareness of that phrase and those goals?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the term. I'm not familiar with what they imply. I'm not familiar with the goals of any sort. Nothing ever reached me as the president of the Municipal Assembly. I was not an MP, I was not a member of the Main Board. However, I did attend that meeting and I can remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How familiar were you with the aims of the SDS in general?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiar to the extent to which they were discussed at the Prnjavor SDS meeting. I was not the president of the SDS in Prnjavor ever or the vice-president of the party. Both the president and the vice-presidents informed us about the reports that they had received from the meetings of the Main Board, which were held up until the spring of 1992, when the work of the SDS was frozen and the party stopped functioning all the way up to the end of the war. The then president, Karadzic, told us that in order to prevent divisions among the people along the party lines at the moment when unity was needed, the work of the SDS party was frozen and it did not become operational again until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about two final topics. The first is: A witness came to this Court called Jasmin Odobasic and alleged, among other things, that you were responsible for his being beaten up. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a lie. Never, ever did I order for anybody to be beaten up. In the second part of his testimony, he said that it was another person who had ordered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So that's a comment on his evidence, so leave that to others. The same witness claimed that you were obstructive in the referendum in 1992 by only allowing one polling station in the middle of Prnjavor to be opened, at the Dom Kultura. Any truth in the fact that you were destructive and tried to rig the election, Mr. Odobasic was saying against you?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic. The general opinion among the Serbs was against the referendum. We estimated the situation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. Answer the question, please, the specific question, and I want a specific answer. Did you try and effectively rig the election by only allowing one polling station to be open?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I now want to move on to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness -- I do know that it was not what you specifically asked him, but you're explaining something about the Serbians who were opposed against the referendum and you said, "We estimated the situation to --" could you please -- you wanted to explain something. Could you please explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We believed that there could be some unpleasant things, and given the number of the Muslim population and those who wanted to vote, we estimated the necessary number of polling stations that could be secured by the police, and that is why I made a decision that a polling station should be open in every village. That was a common practice then, and it is still today. So one polling station per village. And in Prnjavor, I set up one polling station for the town of Prnjavor, because I believed that this would be enough for approximately 1.500 Muslims who wanted to vote and that this was as many as we could provide security for in order to avoid major incidents. And indeed, there were no incidents, there were no disturbances or destructions. The police simply wouldn't allow that. Whether I was wrong or not, whether I should have opened two polling stations, is up to people's views and opinions. In my view, I did exactly what I was supposed to do, and I did it right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what Mr. Odobasic said is right to the extent that you decided, for the reasons you've just given, that in Prnjavor town there would be only one polling station? Yes. Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, instead of the two that they Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My final topic, Mr. Vasic, is the accused in this case, Mr. Krajisnik. Did he come to Prnjavor in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was in Prnjavor in February 1993 and in February 1994 -- 5, and he was also there in 1996, during the election campaign, preceding the elections. And those were the visits that he paid to Prnjavor during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What did he -- in short, what was he doing there in February in 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the meeting was held at the Nacional Hotel. At the time, there was quiet on the front line. All the company directors were called to the meeting, together with the leadership of the municipality. Mr. Krajisnik was not alone. I believe that he was a member of the republican delegation. And the visit was staged for everybody to meet each other. It was part of the protocol. There were a lot of discussions about the economy of the town and the requirements of the town, and its economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, did you receive any orders or instructions from Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received Official Gazettes with the conclusions and orders of the assembly of the Republic. As for the direct contacts with Mr. Krajisnik, we didn't have any of those. We did not receive any orders from him. Our contacts with the top leadership of the Republic mainly boiled down to either the president of the party or a member of the assembly contacting Mr. Karadzic if there was a need to do something or to take some measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As a municipal president, are you able to assess what Mr. Krajisnik's power was within the Republic?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, the power line in the party, there was a joint assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We watched those sessions on TV. He became popular because he was very skilful at chairing those assembly meetings and he prevented the MPs who were members of the SDA from passing decisions that would be against the interests of the Serbian people. That's why he became popular. However, we did not see him as having any power. If anything was required, if any instruction reached us in 1991, that mainly went via the Serbian Democratic Party and President Karadzic, save for the functioning of the Municipal Assembly, which was regulated via the Official Gazettes and other official documents that reached us directly from the Republican Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about 1992? In your last answer, you specifically twice referred to 1991.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred to 1991 because the same was true of the period up to May 1991. And then we were left to our own means. If we needed something, we either discussed things amongst ourselves as presidents of municipalities, Banja Luka, Celinac, Prnjavor, we exchanged experiences, or we had contacts with people from the AR Krajina, although we had opposed to that previously. However, we realised that they might have some information and that they might be useful with providing us with advice. We tried to join ranks as municipalities within the AR Krajina. However, this all boiled down to informal talks and consultations. When it came to making decisions, we were left to our own means and we made our own decisions and we were also physically separated from Sarajevo, which posed a problem to us, as well as it did to the witnesses who have testified before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, when in the beginning of your answer you said, "I referred to 1991 because the same was true of the period up to May 1991," did you have in mind May 1991 or May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have misspoken. What I had in mind was May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I thought, but I just wanted to seek confirmation. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That concludes my examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we'll ask Mr. Tieger whether he's ready to start the cross-examination, I would like to put one question to the witness and seek clarification. Mr. Vasic, you were asked about the Municipal Assembly and whether its -- about its functioning and whether its ethnic composition changed in 1991, 1992. You explained to us that some people were replaced but the gist of your answer was that there was not a real major change in the ethnic composition. Somewhat later in one of your answers, when you were asked about the Crisis Staff, you told us that the Municipal Assembly confirmed or -- well, at least took decisions on the 14th of August, 1992, in which it adopted all the decisions taken by the Crisis Staff. And then you added that this was "the last session of the assembly in a mixed composition." What then did change in the composition after the 14th of August? Was it from then on a mono-ethnic assembly? I did not fully understand the answers, the two of them. What happened after the 14th of August in the assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 14th of August, as you can see on the basis of this report, there were still Croats in the assembly and there was a Muslim there as well. After that, up until the end of the war -- well, the Croat member remained, but I think that only one of the Muslims remained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Here again you said there was a Muslim there as well, talking about the 14th of August. And then you said: "After that, only one of the Muslims remained," which sounds very much the same as far as Muslims are concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to Croats, I am in a position to claim that the Croat member remained until the end. And as to the Muslim member, he was present at that meeting, but I can't say anything with any degree of certainty for latter meetings. But I know he was in Prnjavor, in the town of Prnjavor, almost up until the end of the war. He was not a member of the SDA party, and so he did not receive any instructions to leave the assembly meetings and not attend any more. He was a Muslim member of the SDP party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the other Muslims that did not show up any more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do know that the SDA members, at least this is what the president of the party told me in conversation by the way, as it were, that they had the instructions to leave any positions of authority or government in Prnjavor. And even in the meantime, some of the SDP members were supportive of some SDA ideas, such as Mr. Odobasic, some others as well. The reformist powers remained within the assembly, the SDP, SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we look at the list of those who attended, that's under tab - I think it's 11 - it seems that this list is cut off. It's the last tab. It very much looks as if this is cut off from the whole of this document, because after the August session, there seems to be other sessions which is not part any more of this document. Would you have the whole of the document? I mean, how did you get this one, and would the whole of the document be available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked for this, and one of the employees made a photocopy, and this refers to the period in which the Crisis Staff existed and was fully functioning. Afterwards, we did not have any major problems with the functioning of the assembly, because basically what you needed was a quorum, that is to say, 31 members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would ask the whole of the document to be copied, would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so. In case they managed to find it, and they should be able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any supplementary questions. Could I just say this: That Mr. Stewart is here. He does have a few procedural matters that he'd like to mention today, about five minutes' worth, and he needs to do it today rather than tomorrow. Let's put it like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, this would at least save you. I don't know whether you resolved your problem, yes or no, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. I might as well mention at this point and I indicated to Mr. Josse when we returned, that I would be moving forward with the examination. So I guess I get to have my cake and eat it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I might as well mention that Mr. Stewart took a rather more generous view of the situation than I did, but there we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be hardly of any use to first listen to Mr. Stewart, and then even if he would be as short as he always is, and then start the cross-examination of the witness. Therefore, I'd like to instruct you, Witness, Mr. Vasic, not to speak to anyone about your testimony already given or still to be given. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00, where you would expect that you'll be cross-examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Vasic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't know I had been so generous to Mr. Tieger and I didn't know it was Mr. Josse's name to be -- day to be bad cop. I shall have to look at the schedule again. Your Honour, the -- two points. They're related points, actually. I understand from Mr. Josse to whom I spoke in the course of the morning, that Your Honour raised early on today the question of morning and afternoon sittings and scheduling. And as far as -- and invited an up-to-date preference or detailed preference at least to be expressed by the Defence. Your Honour, the Defence's position is this: We would be entirely content with the alternating schedule which we suggested a few days ago of one week mornings, one week afternoons. If that's not possible, and if it is a question, which doesn't seem likely, given the way that scheduling goes, but if it is a question of in effect electing for one or the other, then, Your Honour, casting aside all personal preferences in relation to this matter, the Defence preference would be extremely strongly then for afternoons, for the reasons that I indicated, because it is really for practical purposes impossible to make any serious headway in consultations with the client if we sit mornings, mornings, mornings, mornings. Because the afternoon sessions at the United Nations Detention Unit are extremely short, and after a court day, very unproductive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'll do is to try to get at least 50 per cent of our sessions in the afternoon, and if for any practical purpose we'd have to decide whether it would be more or less than certainly search for more rather than less.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I simply add this. Your Honour has long experience in this Tribunal. I'm sorry I'm at an awkward angle for Your Honours here this morning. But you'll have to look for me out of a side -- sidelong glance or something. But the -- Your Honours will be familiar with this: That if it isn't done in week on, week off, and if it's done in a more not random way, but it's done in a more mixed-up way, that can be awkward for all concerned sometimes when a witness is an afternoon and then again the following morning. It does cause disruption for all counsel in the case sometimes as far as preparation is concerned and for all concerned, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In my conversations with the officer responsible for scheduling, I very much asked for mornings and afternoons. But especially the month of November is a bit different, where no three courtrooms are available. And sometimes also, especially if less courtrooms are available, sometimes we have to make deals with other Trial Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because sometimes, of course, the Judges have also other commitments apart from sitting in the Krajisnik case, both in the Tribunal, sometimes outside of the Tribunal, and that creates now and then a rather complicated situation. But I do understand that apart from what I just said, that your preference, apart from whether that could be followed for the month of November, would be alternating on a weekly basis rather than on a half weekly basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. May I just add this, Your Honour, that however it is exactly done from the Defence's point of view, it is with respect rather important that we do get at least a significant number of afternoons free of court in the month of November. Otherwise we will fall seriously behind, we will have great difficulty in doing the preparation we need to do with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps as a result you get even a bit more than you ask for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's connected. It's this, Your Honour: That I have said something similar on a number of occasions. Your Honour, even based -- well, may I say straight away, it is an area in which it is appropriate for me to just give some indication of personal position. I did write to the Trial Chamber a little while away. After today, in fact, first thing tomorrow morning, I am going to be away and not available in this case for one week, and back next Wednesday. This is long overdue and this is what I'm doing. I did keep the Trial Chamber informed. That's one of the reasons I do hope to deal with this today because I won't be here tomorrow and I won't be here available for work, apart from - of course, I keep in contact with Mr. Josse - until next Wednesday. Your Honour, it's very early in the Defence case, although of course we've had a rather tough run up to it in many ways. Your Honour, a long time ago when the Prosecution was expected to end on a different date, 22nd of April, and a provisional schedule was put before the parties at that stage by the Trial Chamber, it was contemplated that sittings during the Defence case would be four weeks on and one week off. Now, Your Honour, without -- that's just respect reminding on that. Without saying that that would be satisfactory, Your Honour, the position is I can already see, and I have to express it as what I can see and assess as lead counsel myself, Your Honour, as really part of my submissions. I can already see that the contemplated sitting schedule of -- apart from the week's break that's coming up next week for different reasons and the odd United Nations holiday and the normal Christmas/New Year recess, I can see that the contemplated schedule of sitting week in, week out, Monday to Friday, is going to be impossible for the Defence. It simply is. We do not have the human resources. And it won't make any difference, whatever my negotiations with the Registry, the outcome of those won't make any significant difference to what I'm saying here at all. It obviously must make a difference somewhere, otherwise we wouldn't be bothering, but it won't make a significant difference to this. We do not have the human resources and we do not have the time and we do not have the energy, frankly - we just do not - to cope with that sort of schedule. I know it. It's based on pass experience of this case. It's based on an assessment of just the last few days and the weeks before that. Your Honour, I mention it today simply because I didn't want to come back on the 25th of October and raise this point. I'm raising it today just really to give an indication and to ask that we all give very serious consideration to this matter as soon as is possible, which would be, well, maybe it's before the 25th of October. The Defence would be available, Mr. Josse and I would both be available Friday next week and the Monday before we resume on the Tuesday. And Mr. Josse is actually going to Bosnia, so he's not going to be available in The Hague very much either, because he's going to be away too. We both actually won't be available in The Hague. But, Your Honour, we are ready to explore, of course, we are at the Trial Chamber's disposal to explore and discuss and to present and examine any difficulties. But the simple fact, Your Honour, is that we will not be able to do that. And this trial is not manageable on the Defence side on that sort of schedule. And it does need a little more than just tinkering. I can't see at the moment, Your Honour, that, for example, that contemplated schedule of four weeks on and one week off, I can't see that that will work. It just -- it just won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Stewart. I noticed that the four weeks on, one week off was already relying on a previous schedule, but we've well understood your words and we'll consider whether it will cause us to take any action or to enter into any further conversations with the Defence. And I notice that you're available -- I take it that next week Friday, the Judges might not be available. Perhaps on Monday they are, perhaps not all of them. But we'll see how to proceed and just as you can be reached, of course, the Chamber is always at a place where it can be reached if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we're always reachable in one way or another. That goes without saying. On the other hand, we do - it's part of it - have to have some break. May I simply say, Your Honour, I mentioned the past, but -- experience of the past is valuable for the future, but I am concerned simply about today onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We well understood you. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
